opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so ARC has been incredibly valuable. François really put his finger on something important: the ability to pick up a new abstraction from a handful of examples, rather than having seen a million variations of it during training. But ARC is also quite static. You get a few input-output grids, you infer the transformation, you produce an output grid. That's one slice of intelligence: passive induction from a fixed set of observations.

What Zenna and I have been thinking about with MARA is that a lot of what makes humans smart isn't just inferring a rule from data handed to you. It's that you're dropped into a world you don't understand, and you have to *act* to figure it out. You poke at things, run little experiments, form a hypothesis about how the world works, and then use that model to plan and reach goals. So it's modeling, abstraction, reasoning, and agency together, not in isolation.

Concretely, rather than "here are three examples, give me the fourth," it's more like "here's an interactive environment with its own unfamiliar dynamics. Figure out what's going on and do something useful in it." That forces a few things ARC doesn't really test. One is active information gathering: choosing which experiments are informative. Another is building an actual world model you can simulate forward, rather than just a mapping from input to output. And a third is the closed loop: your model is wrong, you notice that from feedback, and you revise it.

I also think it gets a bit closer to the original spirit of what Chollet was after. If what we care about is skill acquisition efficiency, then the natural setting is an agent acquiring skills in a novel environment, where you can measure how much interaction it needed before it became competent. ARC approximates that with a few demonstration pairs, but the interactive version lets you measure it more directly.

And from my own research perspective, this is where I think program synthesis and these more structured, theory-building approaches really earn their keep. If you can represent your understanding of the environment as something like a program, a compact, compositional causal model, then you can reason about what you don't know yet, design experiments to resolve it, and generalize far beyond what you've seen. Pure pattern-matching approaches can sometimes brute-force a static benchmark, but it's much harder to fake your way through a world you have to actively figure out.

So I don't see it as replacing ARC so much as extending it: taking the core insight about abstraction and few-shot generalization, and putting it in a setting where the learner is also a scientist and an agent.

r001.rationale: It describes MARA as an unfamiliar interactive environment where an agent acts to learn, extending ARC’s few-example generalization.

r002.rationale: It explicitly frames MARA as building a world model that can be simulated and revised from feedback.

r003.rationale: It does not say that interactivity makes synthetic problem generation harder.

r004.rationale: It says pattern matching is harder to fake in an interactive world, but does not present interaction as a constraint that reduces overfitting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so first I should say I love ARC. I think François did something really important with it, which is to pin down a notion of intelligence that's about acquiring a new concept from a handful of examples, rather than about having absorbed the right skill from a huge corpus. And the fact that it's been so stubborn for so long tells you it's measuring something real.

But if you spend enough time with it, you start to notice a few things that bother you, and MARA is partly a response to those.

The first is that ARC is a fixed, finite set of puzzles. That's fine for a benchmark, but it has a shelf life. Once enough people and enough systems have ground against the same roughly thousand tasks, you can't really tell anymore whether a method has learned to generalize or whether the whole field has collectively overfit to the quirks of that particular distribution. So one thing Zenna and I wanted was a generative view of the problem. Instead of a pile of tasks, you have a process that produces tasks, something more like a grammar or a program over worlds, so you can sample fresh problems, control their difficulty, and actually ask questions like, how does performance scale with the number of concepts you have to compose, or with how far the test is from the training examples. That lets you do science on the benchmark rather than just report a leaderboard number.

The second thing is that ARC is purely passive. You get your three or four demonstrations and you have to infer the rule. Humans don't usually learn that way. If I hand you a strange device, you poke it. You form a hypothesis, you try something that would distinguish between two hypotheses, and you look at what happens. That active, experimental side of concept learning is completely absent from ARC, and I think it's actually central to what makes human abstraction work. So in MARA the learner can interact. You can query the world, propose an input and see the output, and the interesting measure becomes not just whether you got the answer but how efficiently you got there. How few experiments did you need, and were they the informative ones? That connects to things Zenna has thought about for a long time around causal reasoning and interventions, and it connects to things I care about around program synthesis, because a good experiment is really a search for the input that best splits your hypothesis space.

The third thing, and this is more subtle, is that ARC tasks are mostly independent of each other. You solve one, you move on, and nothing carries over. But the whole story of human intelligence is that you build up a library. You learn one abstraction and it makes the next one easier to learn. In our earlier work on DreamCoder, that was the whole point, that learning is this ratchet where concepts get consolidated and reused. So we wanted an environment where there's a curriculum, where the concepts are related in a structured way, and where a system that actually learns, in the sense of getting better over time at acquiring new concepts, is distinguishable from a system that's just very good at search on each isolated instance.

So if I had to compress it, ARC asks, can you infer a concept from a few examples? MARA tries to ask something closer to, can you learn how to learn concepts, by experimenting with the world and by building on what you already know? Those are the capacities I think we're really after when we talk about abstraction and reasoning, and I'd like a benchmark where progress on them is measurable and where we can't fool ourselves.

I'll be honest that it's early. There's a real risk with anything procedurally generated that you end up measuring your own generator rather than anything about intelligence, and we're very aware of that. We've spent a lot of time looking at whether humans find the tasks natural, because if people can't do them, then we're not measuring the thing we claim to be measuring. But that's the direction, and I think it's a healthy complement to ARC rather than a replacement for it.

r001.rationale: It says MARA lets learners interact with the world by querying inputs and observing outputs, extending ARC’s few-example concept inference toward learning through experimentation.

r002.rationale: It describes forming hypotheses and choosing experiments to distinguish them, framing the interactive task as hypothesis or model building.

r003.rationale: It discusses procedurally generating fresh tasks, but does not say that making problems interactive makes their generation harder.

r004.rationale: It connects fixed ARC tasks with potential overfitting and proposes generative tasks; it does not present interaction as a constraint that reduces overfitting.

astra-6.text:
I think ARC gets at a really important question: can a system encounter something unfamiliar, work out the underlying abstraction from a few examples, and then use it? That’s a much more interesting notion of intelligence than simply doing well on a distribution you’ve trained on extensively.

But a benchmark gives you a fairly narrow window into that process. You see the examples and the final answer; you don’t necessarily see how the system formed a hypothesis, what evidence would change its mind, or whether it can reuse what it learned.

The way I’d frame the ambition for MARA is to make those questions more central. Can we study abstraction as a process—forming explanations, testing them, and building on them—rather than only scoring the endpoint? ARC is an important starting point. The broader challenge is understanding what makes that kind of learning possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from examples and testing explanations, but does not identify interaction with an environment as MARA’s extension of ARC-style generalization.

r002.rationale: It describes forming and testing explanations, but does not clearly characterize MARA’s interactive task as a model-building exercise.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention synthetic problem generation or that interaction makes it harder.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that requiring interaction constrains the task or reduces overfitting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ARC gets at something really important: can you look at a few examples and infer the underlying rule, rather than just recognize something you’ve seen many times before? But it also bundles together a lot of different problems. You have to figure out what the objects are, what relationships matter, and then what transformation is being applied. When a system fails, it can be hard to tell which of those things went wrong.

The way I think about MARA is as an opportunity to make those questions more explicit and more experimentally tractable. Can we vary the kinds of abstractions a task requires? Can we distinguish learning a new concept from composing concepts you already have? And can we test whether an abstraction actually transfers to a different problem?

So the ambition isn’t simply to produce another score that systems can optimize. It’s to get a clearer picture of what they’ve learned and what mechanisms let them generalize from very little data. ARC is a really useful challenge; we’d like to turn that challenge into something that also helps us understand how to make progress.
